utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Your affirmation still applies, Mr. Ostreni. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall last night, or yesterday afternoon in any case, we left off discussing the Ohrid Framework Agreement, and I suggested to you that rather than putting an end to the war, the Ohrid Framework Agreement was a way to avert one? Do you recall my suggestion to that effect?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you a document, Mr. Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This is Rule 65 ter 1D116, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What will appear in front of you, Mr. Ostreni, is a statement by the president of the United States, George W. Bush, and it follow as a telephone conversation with the president of the Republic of Macedonia, Boris Trajkovski. It's dated the 14th of August of 2001, shortly after the Ohrid Framework Agreement had been signed. I'll read to you what President Bush had to say about the agreement. It said this: "This morning I spoke with my friend President Boris Trajkovski to congratulate him on his courage and leadership in negotiating the political settlement that was signed yesterday in Macedonia. "The settlement promises to strengthen democracy and avert civil war, while protecting Macedonia's territorial integrity and political unit. It addresses long-standing political aspirations of the citizens of Macedonia. It is now up to the Macedonia's assembly to adopt the constitutional amendments and legislations to implement the settlement." Do you agree that as far as the statement of the president of the United States is concerned here, what he says is that the agreement, which is a political agreement, promises to avert a civil war? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what he said in his statement, and there's nothing for me to agree on.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say this: "As I have made clear from the outset of the fighting, the United States stands strongly against those armed extremists who have tried to take democracy hostage in Macedonia. President Trajkovski and I agree that their tactics are despicable and their methods undemocratic." Is it correct that even after the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement on the 14th, at least the United States of America continued to view your organisation not as a valid political entity or negotiator, and not as the party to an armed conflict, but as an extremist group that had sought to take the Macedonian state hostage of its demands? Do you agree that that is what the president is suggesting?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, sir, because the NLA did not want to hold a democracy hostage of its demands. Its demand was for the Macedonian state to become a democratic one, and the fact of this is the signing of the Ohrid Agreement; the demobilisation and handing over of weapons by the NLA; and, of course, the inclusion of all its members in the Amnesty Law and their returning to normal lives. So everything following the Ohrid Agreement denies what you're saying. I was not in position to read that document earlier. Even now it is in English. I cannot understand it completely. But the events following the signing of the Ohrid Agreement says that the NLA was not against democracy; but, on the contrary, it contributed to the democraticisation of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree, sir, at the least that your position in the response that you just gave or the or the suggestion that you just made contradicts the view at least of the president of the US? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're putting me in a position to compare my opinion with a person who is very important in the world, and I don't find this suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, perhaps, you knew also that the United Nations, after the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement, continued to define and to characterise your group in terms of an extremist group. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we had very good contacts with NATO, with the representatives of the EU. We fulfilled all their recommendations and instructions as they came along. It was not possible for to us hand over the weapons before the Harvest operation, because there was no one there to hand over weapons; and when we did so, it was done perfectly well without any remarks. This shows that the NLA respected the positions that were taken by NATO representatives during their talks with Mr. Ali Ahmeti.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, just to answer my question, Mr. Ostreni: Simply, are you aware that after the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement, on the 13th of August of 2001, the Security Council of the UN continued to refer to your organisations as an extremist group? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not important whether I will agree on this or not. You are talking here about a day after the signing of the Ohrid Agreement, about the 14th of August. At that time, we were working towards fulfilling all the obligations take on ourselves as the NLA, so that the implementation of the Ohrid Framework Agreement began, which meant the amendments that were to be adopted by the assembly of the Republic of Macedonia. These amendment would say gradually change the constitution in an institutionalised way.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply for the record, the document from the president of the Security Council is Exhibit 1D15.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Ostreni, is it correct that one of the reasons for the international community to not wish to deal or negotiate with you was the fact that your so-called supreme commander or leader, Mr. Ahmeti, was not only unreliable but mentally unstable. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it will be difficult for you to get an answer from me on this, because I'm not a doctor. I'm not a psychiatrist. I cannot make such an evaluation. But throughout my cooperation with Mr. Ahmeti, I haven't seen any signs of what you are saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, are you aware, perhaps, of the fact that from 1993 to 2002 Mr. Ahmeti received a 100 per cent invalidity allowance from the Swiss authorities because he suffered from a severe case of schizophrenia paranoia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about this. It was in the media; but to me, personally, it has no importance. I do not assess a person based on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct perhaps also that another reason why the international community and the Macedonian authorities also didn't want to negotiate with you or Mr. Ostreni [sic] is because they knew full well that your organisation never had a centralised command system and that your organisation remained connected -- a loosely connected community of little cells or groups? Is that one of the reasons why they didn't deal with you?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It is well known in the entire world that democracy requires for changes to be sought through legal institutions of the state and government. I think that the tendency in the future should also remain the same, that these changes are realised through institutions, legal institutions. In the statement of the United Nations, on human rights and freedoms, there is a stipulation saying that if an ethnic group continues to suffer trampling upon of its rights and exclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- excuse me, you asked me the question and I need to answer it. You asked me why we were not included in the negotiations, and this is something that I cannot answer by simply saying yes or no. This is a very important issue, and I would kindly ask you to allow me to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Ostreni, if you feel have you to add to the answer, please, by all means. The question, however, was more limited in nature. The question was whether the fact that your organisation never had a centralised command system and remained a loosely connected group -- sets of groups or cell is or could be one of the factors why the international community did not wish and did not deal with you as a negotiating partner in?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer your question now. The National Liberation Army had its General Staff and its political representative, which -- who simultaneously was the commander of the NLA. It had a well established hierarchy. This can be proved by the withdrawal from Haracin, when Mr. Ali Ahmeti entered in agreement with NATO, with its representative, Peter Feith; and following this agreement, the battalion was withdrawn from Haracin. We operated through brigades. These brigades were subordinated to the General Staff and to Ali Ahmeti, but what happened was because this was an uprising; and if an uprising is supported in one country, then you have to support it another country as well. The demands of the NLA, laid out in communique number 6, in the memorandum, as well as in all other communiques, are included in the Ohrid Framework Agreement. So I don't see what you're saying here, that the NLA's position was not included and the position of its leadership. This was regulated through the Prizren agreement, through the Albanian political parties that were taking part in these negotiations. They signed this agreement with the approval of the NLA, because there was agreement and regular contact with our political leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. I would like to show you two documents, and then I will ask you a couple of questions on those, Mr. Ostreni. The first one has already been shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's Rule 65 ter 1D1044, 1D1044.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Ostreni, you will see it is already a document that I have shown to you earlier. It's a document - thank you - that comes from up with of the embassy, and the passage that I would like to read to you is at the bottom of the first page in particular. Thank you. It is under number 2, and it reads as follows: "NLA infrastructure is designed and best suited for independent guerilla tactics: A loose organisational structure; low interdependency on other NLA groups and commanders; individual commanders have authority to establish new fighting groups and to evolve fighter structure to meet the military requirement; NLA brigades have similar structure to UCK structure; NLA fighters are divided into independent operational zones; local commanders have decision-making authority; individual commanders have autonomy in planning of attacks within their operational zones." Before I ask you a question about this document as well, Mr. Ostreni, I'd like to show what you is Exhibit 1D260. This is also, Mr. Ostreni, a document that I have shown earlier to you. This is a piece that appeared in Jane's Defence Weekly on the 29th of August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry could go to the second half of the document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Ostreni, in the middle column in the article called, "How many weapons in Macedonian," there's a paragraph starting with the word, "NATO must deal." This is what Jane's Defence Weekly said about the structure, or at least an aspect of the structure of the NLA. It says this: "NATO must deal with the fact that the NLA does not have a fully integrated chain of command nor centralized logistics." And my question based, inter alia, on this document is this: Is it correct that the authority to take decisions as regard the functioning and the activities of your organisation, Mr. Ostreni, was not as you said at the so-called Main Staff level but at the local level of the people who called themselves brigade commander? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander was responsible for his own brigade, while the commander of the NLA was responsible for all the brigades. You asked me two questions. The one previously was about the operational zones. I already explained this. The difference between the war in Kosovo and what happened in Republic of Macedonia was the subordination of the brigades. They were subordinated directly to their commander. The discipline and the collection of weapons of the NLA demonstrates that they followed the orders and the positions of the commander of the National Liberation Army. All the brigades, pursuant to the plan drafted in cooperation with NATO, when the positions where the weapons were to be surrendered were designated, everything was followed, every item of the plan was followed. Not a single unit was apposed to this, and nobody was forced to force others to hand over their weapons. Every soldiers, out of their free will and with a conviction that the Ohrid Agreement has included the demands of the NLA, they surrendered their weapons and they hoped that this will result in the changes to the constitution and the status of the Albanians in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, Mr. Ostreni, that the complete military irrelevance of the Main Staff can be evidenced, for instance, by the fact that neither you nor Mr. Ahmeti was able to provide a single combat order to the Office of the Prosecutor when you met with them? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP did not ask for that. Our orders, in the beginning, were issued during direct contact. When I arrived, some brigades were operative, the 113rd and 112nd, while other tasks were communicated orally. The communication was maintained through satellite phones that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it the truth, Mr. Ostreni, instead that the complete military relevance of the Main Staff, you and Mr. Ostreni [sic] essentially, is also evidenced by the fact that the only map which you were able to provide to the Prosecution, the one that you coloured in yellow and other colours which was shown here, was not even given to any of the brigades? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map was not given to the brigades because it could fall into other hands. Only their respective tasks were given to them; for example, 112th Brigade had its own tasks, the 114th and the 116th as well, they were aware of their tasks. That map consisted of two tasks: The first task which is the beginning, which is marked with yellow; and the second task, which is marked with green, and which indicates the continuation of the operation. If we had a map, as you describe it, that would mean that the NLA started everything like a well-prepared -- pre-prepared army for the war. So everything happened. It developed first smaller units, squads, platoons, battalions to the brigades, and this is how the combat was carried. For example, Izmet Jashari Brigade, on the 1st of May, goes out in the villages of Lipkovo municipality. It takes up position there and it fights. And in such a form of operation, it is quite normal to have just one map, and on the same map to work on the follow-up operation. This is how I say it, operational, and how I view it in a working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it the case also that the complete irrelevance, military irrelevance, of the so-called Main Staff of your organisation may be gleaned from the fact that your organisation was never able to carry out more than hit-and-run attacks, ambushes, and take villagers that had been abandoned by security forces? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I already told you, and I will repeat myself. The NLA was not a ready-made army. It was an uprising that changed gradually into a National Liberation Army. Every day it expanded in manpower with new volunteers; and with time, it was supposed to get to a certain number of people in order to carry out an operation. This is what was being prepared; for example, the operation Liria 2, Freedom 2, which, due to the preparations for the Ohrid Agreement, did not -- was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't the truth, Mr. Ostreni, that the so-called Main Staff of your organisation was essentially a propaganda exercise, whereby you made your organisation look like an army, but in effect the only thing it did was to issue press communiques for propaganda purposes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Let's look now at the laws and regulations which you discussed with the Prosecution and which you say you prepare after having been appointed in March and you said you prepared during March, April, and May. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During March, April, I continued regularly to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Ostreni, that those so-called laws and regulations were, in fact, never prepared, when you say they were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct that they were never in force, never adopted, and never implemented before the 13th of August, 2001? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, because of the following: The units, based on these regulations, acted. They implemented the rules that they could in such circumstances. Some where they slept, they ate. They raised the flag when that was possible in the territory where they were situated. They complied with the orders of the squad commander, platoon commander, battalion commander, company commander, brigade commander. In other words, the regulations were in force regularly. This is a time come pricing of several months. There was a great number of volunteers who had not completed their compulsory military service with the army of the Republic of Macedonia or other armies, but there were also volunteers who had completed the compulsory military service and who were familiar with the military rules, because in whatever army these rules are similar. So, in one word, these rules were being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree, Mr. Ostreni, that the inexistence and non-adoption of these so-called rules and regulations at the time would explain the fact that neither you, nor Mr. Ostreni [sic], nor for that matter other members of your organisation, were able to produce a single document coming from the brigade level that referred back to any of those laws and regulations during the relevant period? Do you agree that's because there was no such laws and regulation in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the rules for the internal service in the armies, they are centralised. The brigade does not draft its own rules, but its the centralised rule book for the army which is implemented, and this is the direction that we followed. If each brigade drafts its own rule book, then that would -- there would be chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that, Mr. Ostreni, but I wasn't referring solely to any draft book. But do you agree that this would explain that not a single instruction, not a single order, not a single map, not a single other combat document from any of the so-called brigade was produced or given by you to the Office of the Prosecutor that referred back to any of those laws and regulations, which you say you adopted during the relevant period and which you say were enforced [sic] at that time?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to military rules, the General Staff is obliged to assign tasks two levels below. The -- each unit is obliged to do the same. So in the documents that I have drafted, I have done it for the brigade and battalion levels. This is how it should work, and the battalion should think about two levels below. So they shouldn't tell us what they do, but they know what they should do to implement -- implement the rules drafted by the General Staff. This is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But isn't it the case, Mr. Ostreni, that you claim to have prepared those rules after your appointment, which you say took place towards the end of March; but, in fact, at that time, Mr. Ostreni, and at that time when you said you prepared those rules, you had not yet been appointed in your position? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. For the rules of service, I also worked when I was in Kosova for the General Staff there. Starting from 1969, I have worked as the Chief of Staff, and it wasn't a problem for me to sit down and draft the rules of service. I started the contacts with Ali Ahmeti at the beginning of March; and then, as we worked, he appointed me to be the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But isn't it the case, Mr. Ostreni, that it wasn't the truth what you said to the effect that you had been appointed as the so-called Chief of Staff of the NLA towards the end of March, but that it took place much later in time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, because in the operation MX, that was about the 20th of March, I was in Vejce together with Mr. Ali Ahmeti, and that shows that much earlier I had started to work with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But isn't that correct, Mr. Ostreni, that your claim that you had been appointed as a Chief of Staff of the NLA at the end of March of 2001, as you have said in your statement and claim before this Chamber, was simply not true?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true. But on -- before the 20th, I was with Ali Ahmeti as the Chief of Staff at the headquarters in Vejce, where now there is a plaque, a commerorative plaque, saying that the General Staff of the NLA worked here. Everybody can see that. It's displayed on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Mr. Ostreni, that your appointment took place in or around the 12th or 13th of May of 2001, and that the purpose of your appointment was to coincide with the announcement of the new Grand Coalition in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You presented here a document which says that I issued a communique about the operation MX in Tetovo, and I signed the communique as the Chief of General Staff of the NLA. The communique was issued in April, after -- after the operation MX. That was after the operation MX in Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Mr. Ostreni, that these regulations, laws, and other names you gave them were prepared, signed, and given to the Office of the Prosecutor long after March, April, and May, as you said?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year are you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a matter of clarification, because the question, I believe, it is not very clear, because first my colleague is asking when the regulations were prepared and when they were given to us. So just not to confuse the witness, these are two different dates and two different questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're quite correct, but I don't think that would have confused this witness, Ms. Regue. Carry on, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Ostreni, that those documents, which were presented to you in your evidence in chief called law, regulations, and other such names, were prepared not before but after the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could that be correct? It's not correct. Because on the basis of these documents, on the basis of these structures that I drafted, I determined the quantities of ammunition and the weapons that they had. Without having a clear idea about the establishment and the structures, I couldn't have calculated how many weapons and how much ammunition the army required. And on that basis, I determined how many Kalashnikovs a unit needed, and then considering that 150 bullets for one rifle. And on the basis of all these quantities, I determined how much was required, and the logistical department determined the further details. And if we had worked on the basis of what you are saying, we wouldn't have carried out the operations that we did. That's why I'm saying that everything was prepared, and now you're forcing me to say that soon after the Ohrid Agreement was signed, we had a meeting with the NATO ambassador in Sipkovica about the responsibilities during the war. There I insisted that you could see a set of all the documents that the NLA had, showing him in confidence, of course, the maps, on the basis of which the operations were carried out, and the map for the operation that was to take place. That is why what you're saying is not correct; otherwise, the NLA wouldn't have reached the Ohrid Agreement and -- and wouldn't proceed along -- along the path that some Macedonian structures were taking. They were giving out weapons to civilians. They distributed 35.000 Kalashnikovs. And if we continued on the same path, things would have taken a very bad turn. But we were determined to -- to follow and take our responsibility in line with -- with the development of the NLA, so that we could have under control all our forces in order to reach our joint goal, which was that the Albanians be a nation-forming entity, so they could enjoy the higher education rights, so that they could enjoy their natural human rights and their freedoms, and those which nobody can dare to infringe upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you know what the EUMM is, Mr. Ostreni?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but the -- those who worked to monitor the situation and had contacts with me. I knew them, and I respected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you agree that they were quite well-informed about what was going on in Macedonia at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about "them." I don't know who are you talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostreni. "Them" being the EUMM, the monitors of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still, it is not clear. I don't know what "EUMM" is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I understand that it stands for European Union Monitoring Mission, and those were the people whom you say you worked with, as the monitors. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have worked mostly with NATO people, because at the time we were working for the preparation of the Harvest operation. As for the political angle, they were dealing with Mr. Ali Ahmeti. I was dealing with the military side of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you just said, a minute ago: "They had contacts with me. I knew them, and I respected them." Is it still the case, Mr. Ostreni?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that all those who worked. When you say "them," "they," I can say all those who worked with me. I have insisted on meeting their demands and working with them to fulfil what they wanted. But when you say "they," it does not determine a specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, you said a moment ago: "Those who worked to monitor the situation and had contact with me, I knew them, and I respected them." The question was about the EUMM. Did you have any meetings with members or representatives of the EUMM during the crisis, Mr. Ostreni?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that, at the time, whoever wanted to talk to me, to meet me, I met them. I can't remember each and every one of them, but I do remember the contacts with the NATO people, because I was working with them on the military side of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show you a document, Mr. Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This is Rule 65 ter 1D1083.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Ostreni, it's a document which is called, "The National Liberation Army in the FYROM," and I'd like -- it's a document that contains some information about your organisation, and I'd like to go to the part that deals with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's the next page, 1D00-8815. If we could scroll down to the bottom of the page, please, and if it could be enlarged somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: See, Mr. Ostreni, this is a sort of short summary. There's a page afterwards of who you are and number of information about you and your activities in the NLA, and it says this: You were born in 1942 in Debar. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which year I was born? 1942, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct. Then it says General-Major chief commander of NLA, and it says appointed 13 May 2001. That's the truth, isn't it, that your appointment took place not on the 30th or around the 30th of March, as had you said -- or at the end of March, as you had said in your statement and in evidence, but on the 13th or around the 13th of May of 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just said two untruths. The first one, whoever wrote this one, has put it wrong, because I was not chief commander of the NLA, as it says here. There are two untruths. First, I was not commander. This was a mistaken assessment, and I was not appointed on the 13th of May but I was appointed earlier, as I said here before. All the notes in this document are just guesswork, it seems to me. I have difficulties in reading it. I could read -- it says there "the main commander of the NLA." I was not the main commander of the NLA. The main commander of the NLA was Mr. Ali Ahmeti. So the document should not be accepted as one with facts from the very start.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Mr. Ostreni, that, in fact, what matters here is the fact that your appointment took place on the 13th of May, 2001, not in March as you have claimed, and that this explains the fact that the regulations or laws, which you said you adopted and prepared in the course of months of March, April, May of 2001, were not, in fact, adopted at that time, but were prepared ex post facto for the purpose of pretending and giving the appearance of a regular army? Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say, sir? The document itself shows that it has got mistaken information. It says that on the 13th of May, I was appointed as the general commander of the NLA, which is incorrect. I have never been the NLA commander, and neither the one -- the first nor the second is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, we have no further questions. The only matter, Your Honour, which is outstanding is the issue of the exhibits. We have discussed it with our colleague. We have given them the list of the documents which we would seek to tender through this witness. I think, at this stage, there is quite a large agreement [sic] between the two parties. But if we were given the time during the break, we could finalise the list, perhaps, and submit to Your Honour, either after the break or, if you wish, at the end of the witness, as suits the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that an opportunity to resolve differences can be well-justified, but we need to deal with the matter before the witness finishes, in case there's some need for any further questioning of the witness about them. Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one question related to the last document. Maybe I missed it, but I'm not quite sure whether my colleague mentioned the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think you missed it. I don't think it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The source, Your Honour, and I'm grateful to the Prosecution, is indicated in another Prosecution document. This is a document that was prepared by the EUMM, and then reused by the Prosecution in relation to its own material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And do you know its date?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is not apparent from this document; but during the break, we can seek from the other documents used by the Prosecution, in which it is referred, whether there's a date to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would like to thank, Mr. Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I have some questions for this witness, but I would first ask for a minute or two to prepare with the written materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you ready, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I will now begin with the questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness, Gzim Ostreni. My name is Antonio Apostolski, and together --

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: -- and together with my colleague, Jasmina Zivkovic, we are defending Mr. Johan Tarculovski. Today, I will present to you a number of questions about the events in Macedonia in 2001. Witness Ostreni, you were born in 1942 in the town of Debar in western Macedonia, a place inhabited with mixed Macedonian and Albanian population. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If you're asking me that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: As part of your mandatory military service in the JNA in 1964, you have completed the military school for reserve officers in Bileca, Bosnia. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bileca of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said. Is this correct, then?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You were then -- you were promoted into lieutenant-major --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: As second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: This is the rank of a reserve officer, of a commissioned officer?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. In 19 --

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because I hear the question in Macedonian, and just instinctively, I reply in Macedonian. But before then, I worked in another village in Sologic in 1961; and then after finishing the reserve military school, and passing the practical exam successfully; then I got the rank; but after that, I worked in the school in Debar.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Therefore, you understand the Macedonian language.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I understand it, but I speak it an a literary way.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you -- did you finish the school University of Sociology in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Skopje but in Pristina. I graduated from the Faculty of Philosophy and Sociology in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Communist Party of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was included without requesting membership.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: As of 1969, when the Territorial Defence Staff was formed in Debar, you became commander of this staff. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you're insisting on my CV, I would like to mention that as of 1964, in Tetovo, I was the chairman of the municipal youth committee; then I worked in the organ of the interior as a secretary of border for the tourists that were entering and leaving the country, for their travelling documents; then in 1969, according to the law, the formation of Territorial Defence units began at a republican level, and they were part of the Territorial Defence Staff of the republican level. Having reviewed my experience and my military expertise, they promoted me and transferred me from the interior organs to the Territorial Defence Staff. So this all occurred as of the sixth month --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter didn't catch the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and this where I worked. So I was Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of a municipality, which, pursuant to the rules, corresponded to the post of chief of a brigade, in military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You retired in the 1991 in the rank major in reserve. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reserve or active, depending on what you do. At the time, I was working directly, pursuant to the military rules; and as all my colleagues, I was treated as a reserve officer because of the salary, but our tasks and competences were the same with the active ones, as envisaged with military rules. I was retired on the 1st of May in 1991 on my own request, because I believed that the situation was getting worse and I no longer wanted to remain in that post, where I would be required to do duties that I was not paid for. That's why I requested a retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: But your rank, major, was in reserve, was not active?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The post that I occupied was corresponding to a lieutenant-general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Lieutenant major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you employ a military, then he is no longer reserve. The state was manipulating with our rights. They were considering as such, due to the payment; while in practice, we were performing other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell me, briefly, whether you were active major or major in the reserve service?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working with the Territorial Defence; and when a summons would be sent for the activisation of the units, this was done according to the laws military roles. So I will repeat again: I was treated as a reserve officer, but I was, in fact, doing a job of an active officer, to work on a mobilisation of -- a mobilisation plan or a wartime plan, to work on a plan of filling in personnel and materiel establishment, to work on a plan of state of readiness. These are all professional duties linked with professional military tasks, but the state regarded as reserve officers because they wanted to pay us as civilians, as reserve officers, not as active military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In March 1999, you joined the units of Ramush Haradinaj in Kosovo, and you became a member of the liberation army of Kosovo. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't go there to join the forces of Ramush Haradinaj, but I went there to join the UCK of Kosovo. So my luck was to go to Mr. Ramush Haradinaj, whom I highly respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, so far, all the questions of my learned colleague are, basically, reproducing the 92 bis statement, which was already admitted into evidence. I was wondering whether which is the relevance and going over an already existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Apostolski is moving quickly to the matters that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I wanted to clear up whether major, as a rank, was a rank which the witness has as an active rank or a rank in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the goal of your going to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent this is linked to these proceedings here, but I will answer your question. At the time, I was in the United States of America visiting my daughter and her family, living there. It was 1998, late 1998; and through radio, TV, and other media, I was hearing reports of fierce fighting going on in the territory of Kosova. The information I received from the media was saying that terror was going on, and victims of this terror were the civilians. So I took the decision to join the Kosovo Liberation Army, and I found the way, how to go there, to contact them and to contribute to them with the duties that I was able to carry out. And after March, I was convinced that it was a good decision to join the UCK of Kosova, because on the 26th of March, NATO undertook its air campaign against the Serb forces in Kosova. So this boosted my morale, because it proved that my decision was not wrong, to join the UCK in Kosova, because the war there was a huge-scale one.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. My participation in Kosova does not exclude the help that Macedonia provided NATO with, because it allowed to use its territory for its preparations. So my participation in the war in Kosova is in line with the policy that Macedonia followed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In 1999, during the war in Kosovo, Macedonia provided refuge for thousands of Kosovars fleeing from there. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But you should use another term here, not leaving Kosova, but expelled from Kosova by the Serb forces. I regret that this term continues to be used in Macedonia because you cannot say they left Kosovo, since they did not leave it out of their free will. They were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In March 2001, when Mr. Ali Ahmeti appointed you as the Chief of Staff, the General Staff was located in Vejce. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We were in Prizren, and at that time we transferred to Vejce.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In April 2001, the General Staff was located in Kosovo, Prizren. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In April, it was in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In May, the General Staff was located in Sipkovica, where it remained until the signing of the Ohrid Agreement.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Because if I remained in Sipkovica, together with Mr. Ali Ahmeti, the contacts with the brigade, operating in a front of 200 kilometres wide, it would have been impossible to have direct contacts and frequent contacts. The situation had to be managed, so Prizren was a suitable location for this job. It is in depth enough to enable one to carry its duties, and it is near the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: The question was: Is it correct that in May the General Staff was located in Sipkovica and remained there until the signing of the Ohrid Agreement?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. There were situations when the political representative or the commander would go to Sipkovica but would return to the command post. In military terms, it is allowed to have a command post, a basic one, then a reserve one. So it's a regular practice. A commander could move wherever he wanted to and wherever he deemed necessary to be at a particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown his statement, 4D-497 [as interpreted], item 22, page 27 of the English and Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see the statement before you? It is in the Albanian language -- in the English language.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you enlarge it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is item 32. Please go further down in the Albanian verse version please.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You state here that, in March 2001, the General Staff was located at Vejce; in April, it was at Kosovo; and, in May, it was Sipkovica, where the General Staff remained until the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement; and, for sometime, the General Staff was illegally located in the city of Prizren. So could you now agree with me that the General Staff of the so-called NLA was in Sipkovica since May and until the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because you're not reading the first part which says: "Elements of General Staff were constantly moving," which means part of the General Staff were constantly moving. There were parts of the General Staff that were located in one location, others in another location. I was in Prizren, and I was Chief of General Staff. Item 32 does not speak of General Staff but it speaks of elements of General Staff. You have seven or eight departments within the General Staff. There is need for them to move, especially need for the commander to move. Personally, until 26th of March, I was in Vejce. After 26th of March, I was in Prizren, and I could work better from there. You have the same paragraph in the English. You have the word "elements" there, so it means "parts" of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you in the General Staff for all the time?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, of course. There were moments when I was requested to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You worked on these documents for organisation of the NLA there?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: During the conflict, in the period between March and August, you were not in Kumanovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the demobilisation, that is, up until the signing of the Ohrid Agreement, I was not. It was not possible for me to leave because by going to Kumanovo or to another brigade would cause my absence from the General Staff for several days or a week, and that would have serious consequences for the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: That means that, during the conflict, you stayed in the General Staff in Vejce, in Prizren, and in Sipkovica throughout the time. You never left those places. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Does this mean that, during the conflict, you stayed in the General Staff for all the time in Vejce, in Prizren, and in Sipkovica, and you never left those locations?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 13th, I went to Sipkovica; so, in Vejce, in Prizren, and after the 13th in Vejce. And from there, I toured 113th Brigade, 115th Brigade, 114th, 116th. The situation was supposed to be followed from a close distance and there were conditions for that, because preparations were ongoing for the handing over of the weapons and for the Harvest operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: During the conflict, you were not in Skopje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "during the conflict." Could you please give me certain dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: The period March to August.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: And you have not drafted any of the documents in Skopje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, in a way, correct, but we would write "Shkup," that is Skopje, in the documents, because at the time we were in Kosova, in Prizren, and we could not write "Prizren" there. Our country was Macedonia. Our army was operating there, and that's why we wrote "Shkup," that is, Skopje, on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: So you misrepresented that the documents were written in Skopje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not misrepresented. This was done deliberately so that the organs would not detect our location. Of course, they knew it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Your commander, Ali Ahmeti, was with you during all times in the General Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all times. There were -- there were situations when he would go to Shipkovice; for example, when the issue of the withdrawal from Haracin occurred, at that time, he was in Shipkovice, then he returned, then he went again to Shipkovice. He remained there, and then I joined him after the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that your commander, Ali Ahmeti, was with you at Kosovo, while the General Staff was at Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was not in Shipkovice, of course, he was together with me in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the statement of Ali Ahmeti, item 32, page 6 of the Macedonian version and the English version is page 6. 65 ter 2D325.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the paragraph 31 of the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you could enlarge please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel and the witness not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: The statement of Mr. Ali Ahmeti was translated into the Macedonian language. You understand the Macedonian language. So you can see that, when asked by the investigators of the OTP where was the General Staff of the NLA located, your commander, Ali Ahmeti, says that the General Staff and the Supreme Command were at Vejce in March, and the Supreme command and the General Staff were moved to Sipkovica in April 2001, where they remained until the end of the conflict. Could you agree with me that your commander says something that does not correspond to what you say, that the General Staff was in Shipkovice in April, and he never mentions that the General Staff of the NLA was in Kosovo sometime.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you the truth. In March, we were in Vejce. After March, after the MX operation, both myself and Mr. Ali Ahmeti returned in Prizren. Afterwards, Mr. Ali Ahmeti, at given times, went to the locations that he mentioned in his statement. Now, whether that is a mistake in the statement or his own mistake, that I cannot say. But what I'm saying here is true, and I can be held responsible for the words that I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: That means that when your commander, Ali Ahmeti, was giving a statement to the investigators of the ICTY, he was not telling the truth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he is not telling the truth. What I said was that a mistake was made, either by the person who took the statement -- I don't know what actually happened. I'm not saying that he is lying. I'm here, the witness. I'm not lying, and I confirm that, in March 2001, we were in Vejce; then we returned in Prizren; and then Mr. Ali Ahmeti went back and was moved to Shipkovice, as he says in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would this be the convenient time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Witness Ostreni, did you have a communication system in your General Staff?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my General Staff, I didn't need to have any communication system because I was there all the time; but, with the brigades, yes. When Ali Ahmeti went to the command headquarters, then we had communications and we would used satellite equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You used satellite phones for your communication. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, satellite equipment, but also the phones which are in use in our everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you use radio communications?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between myself and -- and the brigades, no. We were making preparations to have a system, a radio system, but it wasn't needed because the -- the cease-fire was launched, and we did not pursue that idea through to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Does that mean that the communication within the General Staff did not use radio connections?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the General Staff, we didn't use radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown, again, the statement of his commander, Ali Ahmeti; 65 ter 2D325, item 31, on page 6 in the Macedonian version, and page 6 in the English version as well. Could the bottom part of the Macedonian page be shown, please, and could we please scroll it down, a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: His statement to the OTP investigators, your commander, Ali Ahmeti, says: "We had installed communication system that was operational around the clock. The internal communication was carried out through radio links." So isn't this the opposite of what you testified a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, within brigades, we used the small radio communication systems; but between the General Staff and the brigades, we did not use such radios, but we used satellite phones, and someone has also used the everyday phone lines. Which -- which paragraph are you reading from? You didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: I said it was paragraph 31, item 31, where he speaks about the General Staff, where Ali Ahmeti speaks about the General Staff and tells where the General Staff was located, and then continues to say that: "In the General Staff there was a communication system installed that was operational around the clock, and the internal communication was carried out through radio links." He speaks about the internal communication within the General Staff, as far as I understood.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't understand it like it that. When he was in the 112 Brigade, there they had an internal system of communications; whereas, the contacts with me, he kept by satellite phone, which were functional also for the 112 and the other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: So you are not aware that the internal communication was carried out through a radio links. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to state here that as the Chief of General Staff here, in the General Staff, I have not used radio communication systems to communicate with brigades. The brigades had radio communication equipment to communicate within themselves but not to use it to communicate with the General Staff. I know the person who -- who was in charge of the radio communication system in the 112th Brigade. Now that you're asking, I'm starting to recall details like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: But is it correct that you stated in your evidence that in the internal communication, within the General Staff, you did not use radios?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now I'm saying the same thing. In the General Staff, we did not use a radio communication system to communicate between the departments of the General Staff and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: If you remember, my colleague, the Prosecutor Regue, showed you several documents related to the organisation of the NLA, and you confirmed them to be developed by you in the period between March and May 2001. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which documents you're talking about. Can you show them to me on the screen, please. We've spoken about many documents with Ms. Regue. That would be a good idea to have them in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: You do recall that several documents were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P498.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the following page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see that page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: First, let me ask you: Did you have this document during your interview with the ICTY investigators on the 27th and 29th of July, 2005?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given this document to the -- to the competent people in The Hague, or investigators, as you call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you tell me what does the stamp in the upper left corner of the document mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the upper left corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seal, I can see it clearly. It shows the date when the order was recorded. So if you removed the rest of the document, I could show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: And what does the upper number above the stamp denote?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues...] the lawyer -- it's the protocol number. It's the protocol number, the number of the register, when the document was registered. It was 01-37. As far as I remember, it's the commander, which is -- the commander's orders were a "01," and then "37" is the number of the register in the archives of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: So the number "01" would mean the order by the commander. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You're a lawyer. It shows that it is "01" of the protocol where the document is registered. It just identifies the document. The content of the document is the order itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you stamp all the documents that you had, and did you give them record number?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's normal procedure. If there is a document without a number, that's the fault of a person in the administration who was dealing with it, but all documents should have a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: And could you agree with me that this document was produced in Skopje in 2001?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not drafted in Skopje, but it was drafted in Prizren. I started working on the rules of service in Vejce, and then I continued that work in Prizren, when we moved over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what do the words in the lower left corner mean, "Skopje, 2001."

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The important thing is the year, 2001, and it's the same year under seal at the top, and the note was made to have it "Skopje, 2001," so that the authorities could not identify the location where the command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P489. I apologise, it is a mistake. Could we please show P500, Exhibit P500.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that this document was not registered in the records, as the previous document was? There is no stamp of the records on it.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that it's not registered, but this was the rules of services which was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: So you registered just the orders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instruction was to register all the documents which passed through the archiving department, but sometimes -- sometimes in the archiving department, binders are used. It should have been evidenced. The binders contain more documents in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: At any rate, the orders were supposed to be registered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not an order. It's the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the orders. Were they supposed to be registered in the archives?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 212, R062-6938.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see the document before you in Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: This is an order issued by your commander, Ali Ahmeti, and the document contains several orders, among which also provisions dealing with the accommodation and other further issues. But could you agree with me that this document, again, was not filed by the archive? It contains no stamp.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is one that I recognise. I don't know whether there was a cover for it, but it was produced as is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I think that my colleague is showing Exhibit P499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleague. For the clarification, we were not able to see what was the number under which this exhibit was admitted in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you answer my question: Does this document contain a stamp?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. On the electronic document as shown on the screen, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown now Exhibit P501.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? It was shown to you by my learned colleague from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Albanian version be shown as well.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was shown to me and is evidence of the personnel for the possessions of -- of a squad of 11 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that the document contains no date?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a document of the General Staff, but it's a document created by the units and is just a page of the inventory; and if -- if it was taken for the record then, this should be part of the records for the whole platoon. This is just the evidence, the record for one squad, which is equipped with weapon -- weapons and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: But could you agree with me that this document bears no date? Could you just answer with "yes" or "no," please.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could reply with a "yes" or "no," but I'd like to say that there is no date on this page because it depends on where and how it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that one could not see from this document what company it was related to, what squad, what battalion, and which brigade?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's -- it was -- I drafted these structures of the whole NLA; and at lower levels, they were supposed to draft their own documents. I don't know exactly know what's the origin of this page, this document. It doesn't have a name or any other details identifying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: So you could agree with me that, from this document, it could not be discerned which company, which battalion, and which brigade it was related to?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the person who drafted, this person should know that. He prepared this document for his own use, not for court purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: My colleague from the Prosecution showed you a number of communiques issued by the NLA. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Your organisation, the NLA, appealed to the public with the aim to better inform the public of the goals and the activities of your organisation. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since it's a communique, its purpose is to communicate with the public opinion, with its own members, with the members of the international community, with the public that is in position to accept it and to assess it.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that none of the communiques were not filed in the archives with a seal, as the previous document which we elaborated on just before, which did have a seal?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even to this date, when you communicate with the general public opinion and political entities, the associations, in general, the chairman, they do not seal or stamp their communiques. They release these communiques directly through Internet or to the media; and by the very issuing of the communique, the originator is verified. This is the general practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that some of the communiques were marked with numbers, were numbered? You made mention of communique number 6.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them had numbers; some of them were dedicated to a specific problem; and the content of the communique set out the meaning of that communique, what it was all about. That's why some of them don't have numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that the numbers that were placed on the communiques were placed there without any order or rules?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, the communique number 6 was published. The person who drafted those communiques maybe followed a certain order. But, for me, it was important that they were well composed, that they would convey the message to the general public, and that they would express the general position of the political leadership and the General Staff of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that the numbers on the communiques in your organisation were placed only to create the impression that this organisation existed from before, previously? I ask you concretely in the case of communique number 6, that the number 6 was assigned only to create the impression that this organisation existed from before.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined in March. Whatever existed before that date, that I don't know. What I know is that on the 9th of March, this communique was drafted, and the person who filed it, filed it as communique number 6, the person from the administration. For me, what was important was the content of the communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that, prior to March, the organisation NLA did not exist?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the United States of America. I returned on the 26th. I was in the plane on that date. On the 26th of February, I arrived in Kosovo, and I continued my work. Through the media, at the time, there was information already about the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you, together with your commander Ali Ahmeti, have good cooperation between you?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which time-frame are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time-frame of -- during the conflict, from March, when you joined the NLA, to the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a very good relation, social and professional relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you have a mutual and daily exchange of information between you two?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The counsel is asking whether we had such exchange of information on a daily basis. My answer would be that when the commander, Ali Ahmeti, was at the command post, our exchange of information was daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you ask your commander, Ali Ahmeti, when the NLA was formed?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. My impression was that this was something ongoing, and there was no need for me to ask him that because my work did not depend on that information, as to when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that the NLA does not have a precise date of formation?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is stated also at the amnesty law, so there is no date as from which date those peoples are being amnestied. This is stated by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: When you joined and became the Chief of the General Staff in March, and on the basis of the communique number 6, you had the impression that this organisation had existed earlier. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about an existing organisation. I'm talking about here about an existing uprising. I joined this uprising. Previously, before I went to join the war in Kosovo, I had a meeting with Ali Ahmeti, and I didn't see it in the form and shape that you are seeing it. I simply saw it simply as my patriotic duty. Since people were at uprising, it was my patriotic duty to join them; not to become a Chief of Staff, simply a soldier as all others who joined the uprising. But as Mr. Ali Ahmeti trusted me and believed in my abilities, because he had followed the results of my work in the Dukagjini plain in Kosovo and then at General Staff of the KPC, he entrusted me with the post of Chief of General Staff of the NLA. This was a very difficult and complicated post and task, but I accepted it, and I started to work in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Surely, then, you don't know the contents of the previous communiques with previous numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Would this be your evidence?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I joined, and I simply showed interest in the matters as of the date that I joined the NLA. Before this time, as I already stated, I spent almost two months in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: And you never asked your commander, Ali Ahmeti, what the previous communiques pertained to?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no reasons to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: In any event, you could then agree with me now that when you joined in the March -- in the month of March, and on the basis of communique number 6, you gained the impression that this organisation existed earlier, that it was not formed in the month of March?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question is addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that the uprising was ongoing. That's why I abandoned my post of Chief of Staff of the KPC in Kosovo, as I believed that I could contribute to the further developments of the situation. That's why I voluntarily said that I wanted to join and to be part of the further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you just respond simply with a "yes" or "no." In the month of March, when you joined the NLA, did you have the impression that this organisation existed earlier?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My impression was that there was an ongoing uprising, and that I should give my distribution to the Albanians to whom I belonged in the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it correct that the content of the communiques was fabricated in order to show your organisation, NLA, as an organised army and in order to manipulate the public?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI [Resumed]
